hero.title: Diamond Girdle Guide for Natural Diamond Buyers
hero.subheading: Understand diamond girdle thickness, GIA and HRD grading, durability, setting considerations, hidden weight, girdle damage and the difference between thin, medium and thick girdles.

quickAnswer.title: Quick Answer
introParagraphs: The girdle is the narrow outer edge of a polished diamond where the crown meets the pavilion. It defines the diamond’s outline and normally provides the area gripped by prongs, a bezel or another jewellery setting.

For many modern natural diamonds, a Thin, Medium or Slightly Thick girdle—or a reasonable range across these categories—is generally practical. An Extremely Thin or extensively Very Thin girdle can increase vulnerability to chipping, particularly near corners and points. A Very Thick or Extremely Thick girdle can retain weight without increasing the diamond’s visible face-up size.

The girdle description must not be assessed alone. Buyers should consider where the thin and thick sections occur, the diamond’s shape, setting, measurements, symmetry, condition, complete cut performance and price.

keyTakeaways.title: Key Takeaways
items: The girdle is the outer perimeter separating the diamond’s crown from its pavilion.
Girdle thickness is normally reported as a range from the thinnest to the thickest relevant areas.
GIA uses eight verbal descriptions from Extremely Thin to Extremely Thick.
A range such as Thin to Slightly Thick does not mean the entire girdle has one uniform thickness.
Thin, Medium and Slightly Thick girdles are commonly acceptable, but there is no universal best description for every diamond.
Extremely Thin areas may increase chipping risk, especially at corners, points and exposed positions.
Thick girdles may contain weight that does not contribute meaningfully to face-up size.
A thick girdle does not automatically mean the diamond is poorly cut or unattractive.
Faceted, polished and bruted describe the girdle’s finish, not its thickness.
A faceted girdle is not automatically better than a polished or bruted girdle.
Painting and digging out describe variations created by the relationship between the upper- and lower-half facets around the girdle.
Chips, cavities, naturals, indented naturals and bearding must not be confused with ordinary girdle thickness.
A laser inscription on the girdle can help match a diamond to its report, but it is not sufficient identification on its own.
Fancy shapes require special attention at vulnerable corners and points.
Girdle thickness cannot prove that a diamond is natural rather than laboratory-grown.
Price must be based on the complete diamond, not a fixed girdle discount or premium.

importantBuyerNote.title: Important Buyer Note
paragraphs: This guide explains how girdles are described and assessed. It does not replace examination of the actual diamond by a qualified gemmologist or experienced diamond professional.
A grading report describes the diamond when it was examined. It does not guarantee that the girdle has remained undamaged since the report was issued.

whatIs.title: What Is a Diamond Girdle?
introParagraphs: The girdle is the narrow perimeter around a polished diamond where the upper crown and lower pavilion meet.
Viewed from above, the girdle defines the diamond’s outline. It determines whether the polished stone appears:
closingParagraphs: Viewed from the side, the girdle appears as the dividing edge between the crown and pavilion.

richClosingParagraphs.value: GIA describes the girdle as the middle portion of the diamond and the part normally used as the setting edge. Its thickness contributes to durability and weight distribution.

subsections.title: Is the Girdle a Facet?
paragraphsBefore: Not necessarily.
The girdle may be:
paragraphsAfter: A faceted girdle contains a sequence of small polished surfaces. A polished girdle may be smooth rather than divided into individual facets. A bruted girdle generally has a frosted or granular appearance created during the shaping process.

subsections.title: Is the Girdle the Same as the Crown?
paragraphsBefore: No.
The crown is the complete upper portion of the diamond above the girdle. The girdle forms the boundary beneath it.

subsections.title: Is the Girdle the Same as the Pavilion?
paragraphsBefore: No.
The pavilion is the lower portion below the girdle, extending towards the culet or other pavilion termination.

subsections.title: Is the Girdle the Same as a Lower-Girdle Facet?
paragraphsBefore: No.
Lower-girdle facets, also called lower-half facets, are pavilion facets extending upwards towards the girdle. They are not the girdle itself.

whereLocated.title: Where Is the Girdle Located?
introParagraphs: The principal parts of a polished Round Brilliant are:
closingParagraphs: The table sits at the top. The crown descends from the table to the girdle. The pavilion continues beneath the girdle towards the culet.
The girdle surrounds the entire diamond horizontally.
In a mounted diamond, parts of the girdle may be:
positionBullets: Hidden by a halo or surrounding metal
Positioned above or below the surrounding jewellery
Difficult to inspect without removing or adjusting the setting
finalParagraphs: A complete inspection must account for the areas hidden by metal.

whatDoes.title: What Does the Diamond Girdle Do?
introParagraphs: The girdle has several related functions.

subsections.title: Defines the Diamond’s Outline
paragraphsBefore: The girdle establishes the shape visible when the diamond is viewed face-up.
Variations in the outline may affect:

subsections.title: Separates the Crown and Pavilion
paragraphsBefore: The girdle forms the transition between the diamond’s upper and lower sections.
Its thickness contributes to:

subsections.title: Provides the Setting Edge
paragraphsBefore: Prongs, bezels and other mounting components normally secure the diamond around its girdle.
For that reason, setters must consider:
bullets: Whether an inscription needs to remain visible
The pressure required to secure the stone

subsections.title: Protects the Diamond’s Edge
paragraphsBefore: A properly proportioned girdle provides material between the crown and pavilion.

If the girdle becomes extremely thin or knife-edged, the edge may be more vulnerable to chipping. If it is unnecessarily thick, it may retain weight that contributes little to the diamond’s visible spread.

subsections.title: Is the GIA Scale a Quality Scale?
paragraphsBefore: Not by itself.
The terms describe thickness. Their buying significance depends on:
paragraphsAfter: Medium is not automatically superior to every Thin or Slightly Thick girdle. Similarly, a Very Thick area does not automatically make a diamond unsuitable.

subsections.title: Can GIA Report a Single Description?
paragraphsBefore: Yes.
If the thinnest and thickest relevant girdle areas fall within the same category, the report may show one description, such as:
paragraphsAfter: More commonly, the report provides a range such as:
Thin to Medium
Medium to Slightly Thick
Very Thin to Thick

rangesReported.title: How Are Diamond Girdle Ranges Reported?
introParagraphs: A description such as Thin to Slightly Thick represents the observed minimum and maximum relevant girdle thicknesses.
It does not mean:
bullets: Half the girdle is Thin and half is Slightly Thick
Every area between the two descriptions is equally represented
The diamond cannot receive a high cut grade

subsections.title: How Should a Girdle Range Be Read?
paragraphsBefore: The first term is the minimum thickness. The second is the maximum.

subsections.title: Does a Wide Range Mean the Girdle Is Bad?
paragraphsBefore: Not automatically.
A wider range requires examination because it may result from:
bullets: Normal variation around a scalloped girdle
The design of a fancy shape
Extra material near a corner or point
Cutting decisions used to retain weight
paragraphsAfter: The location and extent of the variation matter more than the width of the verbal range alone.

subsections.title: Can One Small Area Determine the Minimum Description?
paragraphsBefore: A limited area can influence the reported minimum, although laboratory methodology also considers characteristics interrupting the girdle.

GIA explains that features such as a natural, cavity, chip or extra facet may narrow the girdle locally. The remaining girdle and any true knife-edge area must be assessed according to the laboratory’s methodology.
Therefore, do not assume that a report stating Very Thin means the entire girdle is Very Thin.

percentages.title: Diamond Girdle Percentage
introParagraphs: For a Round Brilliant, girdle thickness can be expressed relative to the diamond’s average girdle diameter.
The supporting formula is:
Girdle thickness percentage = girdle thickness ÷ average girdle diameter × 100
GIA distinguishes between two related assessments:
bullets: Average thickness measured at the eight bezel-and-pavilion-main hill positions
Minimum and maximum thickness visually assessed at the thinner valley positions

richClosingParagraphs.value: GIA reports the average hill-position percentage to the nearest 0.5%. The verbal range is based on the relevant minimum and maximum valley areas.

subsections.title: What Are Hill and Valley Positions?
paragraphsBefore: A brilliant-cut diamond has a scalloped girdle.
Hill positions are thicker areas where bezel facets and pavilion-main facets meet.
Valley positions are thinner areas associated with the upper- and lower-half facet junctions.
Because these positions measure different parts of the girdle, an average percentage must not be treated as a direct translation of the verbal minimum-to-maximum range.

subsections.title: Can Buyers Convert GIA Percentages Into Exact Verbal Grades?
paragraphsBefore: Not reliably.
GIA states that:
bullets: Its published percentage examples are approximate
Extremely fine measurements are affected by instrument tolerance
Clarity characteristics may interfere with measurement
The girdle may not be perpendicular to the table
paragraphsAfter: For this reason, use the laboratory’s stated description rather than applying a self-created conversion table.

subsections.title: Does a Higher Percentage Always Mean a Worse Diamond?
paragraphsBefore: No.
A higher girdle percentage indicates more thickness, not complete diamond quality.
Its effect must be assessed alongside:

hrdMeasurements.title: HRD Antwerp Girdle Measurements
introParagraphs: HRD Antwerp commonly reports the girdle using a verbal description, percentage and finish.
Under its January 2025 guidance, HRD uses the following descriptive ranges:
closingParagraphs: HRD separately evaluates how the percentage contributes to the Round Brilliant proportions grade:

proportionsTable.caption: HRD girdle percentage and proportions categories

finalParagraphs: These classifications describe the girdle’s contribution to HRD’s proportions assessment. They do not determine the complete grade by themselves.

HRD also considers crown angle, pavilion angle, table width, crown height, pavilion depth, total depth, culet, polish, symmetry and other observable effects. The complete methodology appears in the HRD Antwerp 2025 cut-grade chart.

subsections.title: Why Is HRD Relevant to European Buyers?
paragraphsBefore: HRD Antwerp reports are frequently encountered in Belgium and the wider European diamond market.
Buyers must recognise that:
bullets: GIA and HRD report formats differ
GIA’s verbal range is not a direct mathematical equivalent of HRD’s percentage
The complete report must be interpreted according to the issuing laboratory

table.caption: GIA versus HRD Antwerp girdle reporting

Extremely Thin through Extremely Thick, including Slightly Thick
Not shown as a separate category in the January 2025 chart

May state faceted, polished or bruted
May state faceted, polished or another applicable finish
Read the complete range, average percentage, finish and overall report
Read the percentage, description, proportions grade and complete report

subsections.title: Can GIA and HRD Grades Be Converted Directly?
paragraphsBefore: No.
Do not assume:
bullets: GIA Medium always equals one HRD percentage
GIA Slightly Thick always equals HRD Medium or Thick
GIA Very Thin always has the same cut implication as an HRD percentage
Identical percentages guarantee identical overall cut grades
A verbal description has the same boundaries across laboratories
paragraphsAfter: Treat each report according to the issuing laboratory’s published methodology.

introParagraphs: There is no single best girdle description for every natural diamond.
For many modern Round Brilliant diamonds, the following descriptions are commonly practical:
closingParagraphs: These ranges often provide a reasonable balance between durability and weight efficiency.
However, the correct decision still depends on:

subsections.title: Is Medium the Best Girdle Grade?
paragraphsBefore: Medium is often considered a balanced result, but it is not automatically better than Thin or Slightly Thick.
A diamond with a Thin to Medium girdle may outperform or offer better value than a diamond with a uniform Medium girdle.

subsections.title: Can Slightly Thick Be Excellent?
paragraphsBefore: Yes.
A Slightly Thick area can be compatible with an attractive, well-cut diamond. The overall assessment depends on the complete proportion set and visual performance.

subsections.title: Can Thick Be Acceptable?
paragraphsBefore: Yes.
A Thick girdle may be acceptable when:
bullets: The shape benefits from additional material at vulnerable areas
The price reflects the complete diamond

subsections.title: Should Buyers Reject Every Very Thin or Very Thick Range?
paragraphsBefore: No.
Both deserve closer examination, but neither should be rejected using the report label alone.

thinGirdles.title: Thin, Very Thin and Extremely Thin Girdles
introParagraphs: A thin girdle contains less material between the crown and pavilion.

subsections.title: Is a Thin Girdle Dangerous?
paragraphsBefore: Not automatically.
Thin is a recognised grading description and is common in marketable diamonds. The concern increases when the girdle becomes:
bullets: Very thin at a corner or point
Very thin next to a large feather
Subjected to pressure during setting or repair

subsections.title: Why Can a Thin Girdle Chip?
paragraphsBefore: Diamond is highly resistant to scratching, but it is not impossible to chip.
A thin edge contains less material to absorb or distribute an impact. GIA warns that very thin areas, particularly at the corners and points of fancy shapes, have a greater risk of damage.

subsections.title: Does Very Thin Mean the Diamond Is Already Damaged?
paragraphsBefore: No.
Very Thin describes thickness. It does not automatically mean a chip, cavity or fracture is present.
The actual condition must be inspected.

subsections.title: Is a Localised Very Thin Area Acceptable?
paragraphsBefore: It may be.
Consider:
paragraphsAfter: A small Very Thin area protected by a suitable setting may present a different risk from an exposed knife-edge running around a substantial part of the diamond.

subsections.title: Can an Extremely Thin Girdle Receive a High Cut Grade?
paragraphsBefore: Girdle thickness is one of several factors in cut assessment. An unusually thin girdle can limit a Round Brilliant’s grade because of durability risk, even when other proportions are attractive.
Do not infer the final grade from thickness alone. Read the grade stated on the laboratory report.

thickGirdles.title: Thick, Very Thick and Extremely Thick Girdles
introParagraphs: A thick girdle retains more material around the diamond’s perimeter.

subsections.title: Why Can a Thick Girdle Be Undesirable?
paragraphsBefore: A thick girdle may add carat weight without producing an equivalent increase in face-up dimensions.
Two diamonds can have the same carat weight but different visible size because one carries more weight in:

subsections.title: Does a Thick Girdle Make a Diamond Look Smaller?
paragraphsBefore: It can.

If a substantial amount of the diamond’s weight is concentrated in the girdle, the face-up diameter or length-and-width measurements may be smaller than those of a more efficiently proportioned diamond of the same weight.
This is why buyers must compare actual millimetre measurements rather than relying on carat weight alone.

subsections.title: Does a Thick Girdle Reduce Sparkle?
paragraphsBefore: Not automatically.
Girdle thickness primarily affects:
paragraphsAfter: The diamond’s brightness, fire and scintillation depend on the complete relationship between its crown, pavilion, table, facet pattern and viewing environment.
An excessively thick girdle may accompany poor weight distribution, but the girdle label alone does not determine sparkle.

subsections.title: Is a Very Thick Girdle More Durable?
paragraphsBefore: It may provide more material at the edge, but it does not make the diamond damage-proof.
Damage can still occur through:

subsections.title: Can Thickness Be Useful at a Fancy-Shape Point?
paragraphsBefore: Yes.

Additional material near the point of a Pear, Marquise or cornered diamond may help avoid an extremely vulnerable knife edge. However, excessive bulging or unnecessary thickness can still retain weight.
The complete outline and setting should be examined.

uneven.title: Uneven and Varying Diamond Girdles
introParagraphs: A diamond’s girdle is rarely perfectly uniform.
Normal variation occurs because brilliant-style girdles are scalloped and because fancy shapes require different facet arrangements around their outlines.

subsections.title: When Does Variation Become Important?
paragraphsBefore: Variation deserves closer attention when it produces:
bullets: Extremely Thin and Very Thick areas on the same diamond
Abrupt changes rather than gradual transitions

subsections.title: Does Uneven Thickness Affect Symmetry?
paragraphsBefore: It can.

GIA considers girdle-thickness variation when evaluating symmetry and when assessing painting or digging out. HRD also lists deviation in maximum and minimum girdle thickness among visual symmetry considerations.
A range alone does not establish the symmetry grade. Read the laboratory’s reported symmetry result.

subsections.title: What Is a Wavy Girdle?
paragraphsBefore: Wavy girdle is an informal expression that may describe visible changes in girdle level or thickness.
Possible causes include:
paragraphsAfter: The term is not a substitute for a laboratory description.

subsections.title: What Is a Sloping Girdle?
paragraphsBefore: A sloping girdle occurs when the girdle plane is not level relative to the table or the diamond’s intended axis.
It may affect:

finish.title: Faceted, Polished and Bruted Diamond Girdles
introParagraphs: Girdle thickness and girdle finish are separate characteristics.

table.caption: Girdle finish types
rows: Series of small polished surfaces around the girdle
Common in modern diamonds; examine facet consistency and inscription
Smooth polished band without separately visible girdle facets
Frosted or granular surface created during shaping
Common in older and some modern diamonds; not automatically a defect
Only part of the girdle has been faceted
May be intentional, repaired or considered during symmetry assessment
Fine feather-like features extend from the girdle into the stone
A clarity and condition consideration, not an ordinary finish category

closingParagraphs: GIA states that girdle thickness is assessed using the same thickness method whether the girdle is bruted, polished or faceted.

subsections.title: Is a Faceted Girdle Better?
paragraphsBefore: Not automatically.
A faceted girdle may offer:
bullets: A suitable area for laser inscription
paragraphsAfter: However, it does not guarantee:
Better cut
Better symmetry
Better polish
Greater durability
Natural origin
Higher value

subsections.title: Is a Bruted Girdle Bad?
paragraphsBefore: No.
A bruted girdle may be completely legitimate. It can also be characteristic of certain older cutting periods.
Inspect it for:
bullets: Compatibility with the claimed age of an antique diamond
paragraphsAfter: A faceted girdle on an old diamond may represent later repolishing rather than the diamond’s original condition. GIA has documented antique diamonds whose original bruted girdles were later faceted.

subsections.title: What Does Partly Faceted Mean?
paragraphsBefore: It means only part of the girdle has been divided into polished girdle facets.
Possible explanations include:
paragraphsAfter: The buyer should compare the current diamond with its report and any historical documentation.

paintingDigging.title: Painting and Digging Out
introParagraphs: Painting and digging out are cutting techniques that alter the relationship between the upper- and lower-half facets and the girdle.

subsections.title: What Is Painting?
paragraphsBefore: During painting, the cutter tilts the upper- or lower-half facets towards the bezel facets or pavilion mains.
This changes the relative thickness between:
paragraphsAfter: The girdle may appear more heavily scalloped in a particular direction.

subsections.title: What Is Digging Out?
paragraphsBefore: Digging out is the opposite relationship.

The upper- or lower-half facets are tilted away from the bezels or pavilion mains and towards each other. This makes the girdle thinner at the half-facet junctions relative to the bezel-and-main positions.

subsections.title: Why Are These Techniques Used?
paragraphsBefore: Possible reasons include:
bullets: Removing a clarity characteristic near the girdle

subsections.title: Are Painting and Digging Always Bad?
paragraphsBefore: No.
Minimal variation can be present without creating a meaningful visual problem.
As painting or digging becomes stronger, it can affect:
paragraphsAfter: GIA calculates the extent of these features using three-dimensional measurement and incorporates sufficiently strong effects into its cut assessment. GIA’s finish and girdle booklet provides diagrams of both techniques.

subsections.title: Can Buyers Identify Painting From a Photograph?
paragraphsBefore: Not reliably.
Controlled imaging may suggest unusual girdle scalloping, but accurate assessment requires:
paragraphsAfter: Do not diagnose painting or digging from one rotating-video frame.

damage.title: Girdle Damage and Clarity Characteristics
introParagraphs: Girdle thickness does not describe the complete condition of the edge.
The girdle may contain or intersect with:

richClosingParagraphs.value: GIA’s diamond-inclusion reference distinguishes bearded girdles, cavities, chips, bruises and other clarity characteristics. See

subsections.title: Is a Natural the Same as Damage?
paragraphsBefore: No.
A natural is retained rough-diamond surface. It is not necessarily damage.
Its significance depends on:
bullets: Whether it makes the girdle excessively thin

subsections.title: Is an Indented Natural Worse?
paragraphsBefore: An indented natural extends beneath the intended polished surface.
It generally deserves more attention than a shallow natural because it may affect:
paragraphsAfter: It is not automatically unacceptable.

subsections.title: What Is a Bearded Girdle?
paragraphsBefore: A bearded girdle contains very small feather-like features extending from the girdle surface into the diamond.
Bearding can result from aggressive bruting or other cutting stress.
Its significance depends on:
bullets: Whether it forms a grey or fuzzy edge

subsections.title: Can Girdle Damage Occur After Grading?
paragraphsBefore: Yes.
Possible causes include:
bullets: A loose stone moving in its setting
paragraphsAfter: If the present condition differs from the report, professional re-examination may be necessary.

inscriptions.title: Laser Inscriptions on the Diamond Girdle
introParagraphs: A laboratory report number, brand mark, symbol or message may be laser-inscribed on the girdle.

subsections.title: What Is the Purpose of a Girdle Inscription?
paragraphsBefore: It can help:
bullets: Match a diamond to its grading report
Identify the issuing laboratory’s report number
Distinguish one diamond from similar stones
Record a brand or personal message
paragraphsAfter: GIA explains that a report-number inscription can be viewed under magnification and checked through its report-verification system.

subsections.title: Does Every Diamond Have an Inscription?
paragraphsBefore: No.
A natural diamond may be:
bullets: Inscribed in an area hidden by the setting
Too small or positioned in a way that makes inspection difficult

subsections.title: Does an Inscription Prove the Diamond Matches the Report?
paragraphsBefore: Not by itself.
A complete match should consider:
paragraphsAfter: An inscription should be treated as one identifying feature, not the entire verification process.

subsections.title: Can an Inscription Be Removed?
paragraphsBefore: It may be reduced or removed through repolishing of the girdle.
If an expected inscription is missing, possible explanations include:
bullets: The inscription is hidden by a prong
The magnification or lighting is inadequate
The diamond does not match the report
paragraphsAfter: Investigate before reaching a conclusion.

subsections.title: Can an Inscription Affect Clarity?
paragraphsBefore: A properly applied report inscription is normally microscopic and placed on the girdle for identification. Read the laboratory report and obtain professional inspection if the inscription appears unusually deep, altered or associated with surface damage.

shapes.title: Girdles in Different Diamond Shapes
introParagraphs: The same thickness description can have different implications depending on diamond shape.

subsections.title: Round Brilliant Diamonds
paragraphsBefore: Round diamonds distribute their outline without sharp corners.
For many modern Round Brilliants, practical ranges include:
paragraphsAfter: Assess the girdle alongside:
Cut grade
Diameter
Total depth
Painting or digging
Symmetry
Face-up performance

subsections.title: Oval Diamonds
paragraphsBefore: An Oval’s girdle may vary around its shoulders and ends.
Inspect:
bullets: Very thin areas near the ends
paragraphsAfter: GIA notes that an excessively thick Oval girdle may retain weight, while an Extremely Thin area can increase vulnerability.

subsections.title: Pear-Shaped Diamonds
paragraphsBefore: Pear diamonds have one rounded end and one vulnerable point.
Check:
paragraphsAfter: A V-shaped prong or another appropriately designed protective setting may be considered for the point.

subsections.title: Marquise Diamonds
paragraphsBefore: Marquise diamonds contain two vulnerable tips.
Inspect:
paragraphsAfter: A girdle that is Very Thin at either point requires particular attention.

subsections.title: Princess-Cut Diamonds
paragraphsBefore: Princess diamonds have sharp corners that can be vulnerable to chipping.
Check:
bullets: Whether the corners are fully protected
paragraphsAfter: Do not judge a Princess solely by its average girdle percentage.

subsections.title: Cushion Diamonds
paragraphsBefore: Cushions can have:
bullets: Modern brilliant or modified facet patterns
paragraphsAfter: Assess the relationship between girdle thickness, outline, faceting and face-up spread.

subsections.title: Emerald and Asscher Cuts
paragraphsBefore: Step cuts have broad facets and different pavilion structures from Round Brilliants.
Inspect:
paragraphsAfter: Do not apply a Round Brilliant cut rule mechanically to a step cut.

subsections.title: Heart-Shaped Diamonds
paragraphsBefore: Examine:
paragraphsAfter: The cleft and point may require different setting considerations.

subsections.title: Antique Diamonds
paragraphsBefore: Old Mine and Old European diamonds may have:
paragraphsAfter: These features must be assessed in the context of age, originality, condition and value.
Do not automatically repolish an antique girdle. Alteration may:
Reduce carat weight
Change the outline
Remove historic character
Affect documentation
Change compatibility with the original setting
Alter market value

settings.title: Girdle Thickness and Jewellery Settings
introParagraphs: The girdle is normally the point of contact between the diamond and its setting.

subsections.title: Prong Settings
paragraphsBefore: Prongs grip selected areas around the girdle.
Consider:
bullets: Whether a prong sits on an Extremely Thin area
Whether setting pressure is concentrated near a feather
Whether corners and points are protected
Whether prongs are worn or damaged

subsections.title: Bezel Settings
paragraphsBefore: A bezel surrounds much or all of the girdle.
Potential advantages include:
paragraphsAfter: However, bezel setting still requires skilled work. Pressure during manufacture can damage a vulnerable girdle, and the metal may hide existing characteristics.

subsections.title: Halo Settings
paragraphsBefore: A halo can reduce direct access to the centre diamond’s girdle.
Check:
bullets: Clearance between centre and surrounding stones
Whether another diamond contacts the centre stone

subsections.title: Tension and Semi-Tension Settings
paragraphsBefore: These designs may apply concentrated pressure at limited contact points.
Suitability must be determined by a jeweller familiar with:

subsections.title: Does a Thin Girdle Require a Bezel?
paragraphsBefore: Not automatically.
The appropriate setting depends on the location and extent of the thin area and the complete diamond. Obtain advice based on the actual stone.

subsections.title: Can a Thick Girdle Cause Setting Problems?
paragraphsBefore: It can.
Possible issues include:
paragraphsAfter: A custom or properly adjusted setting may resolve these issues.

price.title: Girdle Thickness, Face-Up Size and Diamond Price
introParagraphs: Girdle thickness can influence value, but there is no fixed adjustment formula.

subsections.title: Weight Ratio and Face-Up Size
paragraphsBefore: Carat measures weight, not visible diameter.
A diamond with a Very Thick girdle may weigh more than another diamond with similar face-up dimensions because more material is retained around its edge.
Compare:

subsections.title: Can a Thick Girdle Help a Diamond Reach One Carat?
paragraphsBefore: It can contribute to weight retention near commercial thresholds such as:
paragraphsAfter: However, the girdle is only one possible source of retained weight.
A one-carat diamond with inefficient proportions may face up smaller than a lighter, better-spread diamond.

subsections.title: Does a Thin Girdle Make a Diamond Look Larger?

finalTakeaway.title: Final Takeaway
introParagraphs: The girdle is the narrow outer edge separating a diamond’s crown and pavilion.
Its thickness affects three principal buying considerations:
Durability
Weight distribution
Setting suitability

For many modern natural diamonds, Thin, Medium and Slightly Thick ranges provide a practical balance. An Extremely Thin or extensively Very Thin girdle deserves closer attention because vulnerable areas may be more susceptible to chipping. A Very Thick or Extremely Thick girdle deserves comparison because it may retain carat weight without improving face-up size.
The reported range must be examined rather than averaged. A description such as Very Thin to Thick provides minimum and maximum categories; it does not mean the complete girdle is Medium.
Finish must also be considered separately. Faceted, polished and bruted describe how the girdle surface was completed, not whether its thickness is suitable.
Most importantly, do not ask only:
What girdle grade is written on the report?
Ask:
Where are the thinnest and thickest areas, is the girdle undamaged and suitable for the setting, and does the complete diamond justify its weight and price?

faqs.title: Frequently Asked Questions About Diamond Girdles

items.question: What is the girdle of a diamond?
items.answer: The girdle is the narrow outer edge where the diamond’s crown meets its pavilion. It defines the outline and usually provides the edge used to secure the diamond in jewellery.

items.question: Where is the girdle located?
items.answer: It runs around the complete perimeter of the diamond between the crown and pavilion.

items.question: What does girdle mean on a diamond report?
items.answer: It describes the thickness and sometimes the finish of the diamond’s outer edge.

items.question: What is the GIA girdle scale?
items.answer: GIA uses Extremely Thin, Very Thin, Thin, Medium, Slightly Thick, Thick, Very Thick and Extremely Thick.

items.question: What is the best diamond girdle thickness?
items.answer: Thin, Medium and Slightly Thick—or reasonable ranges involving these descriptions—are commonly practical. The best result depends on the diamond’s shape, proportions, condition and setting.

items.question: Is Medium the ideal girdle?
items.answer: Medium is a balanced description but is not automatically better than every Thin or Slightly Thick girdle.

items.question: Is Thin to Medium a good girdle?
items.answer: It is commonly acceptable when the girdle is undamaged and appropriate for the diamond’s shape and setting.

items.question: Is Medium to Slightly Thick good?
items.answer: It can be completely acceptable. Check face-up size, total depth, cut and price.

items.question: Is Thin to Slightly Thick acceptable?
items.answer: Yes, provided the variation does not create durability, symmetry, weight or setting concerns.

items.question: Is Very Thin to Medium bad?
items.answer: Not automatically. Locate the Very Thin area and determine its extent, nearby inclusions and setting exposure.

items.question: Is a Very Thin girdle dangerous?
items.answer: It may increase chipping risk, especially at points, corners or areas near surface-reaching inclusions. The actual risk depends on the diamond.

items.question: Will a Very Thin girdle definitely chip?
items.answer: No. It indicates increased vulnerability, not guaranteed damage.

items.question: What is an Extremely Thin girdle?
items.answer: It is a girdle with little or no material in one or more relevant areas. It requires close durability and setting assessment.

items.question: What is a knife-edge girdle?
items.answer: It is an area where the crown and pavilion meet with effectively no girdle between them, creating a very sharp edge.

items.question: Is a Thick diamond girdle bad?
items.answer: Not necessarily. A Thick girdle may be acceptable, but buyers should compare face-up dimensions and weight distribution.

items.question: Does a Thick girdle make a diamond look smaller?
items.answer: It can if substantial carat weight is retained around the girdle rather than contributing to face-up dimensions.

items.question: Is Very Thick to Extremely Thick bad?
items.answer: It deserves careful comparison because it may add hidden weight and total depth. It does not automatically make the diamond unattractive.

items.question: Does a Thick girdle improve durability?
items.answer: It may provide more edge material, but the diamond can still be damaged by impact, inclusions or unsuitable setting pressure.

items.question: Does girdle thickness affect sparkle?
items.answer: It does not independently determine sparkle. The complete crown, pavilion, facet pattern and proportions determine light performance.

items.question: Does girdle thickness affect cut grade?
items.answer: Yes. Excessively thin or thick girdles can limit the cut grade of a qualifying Round Brilliant through durability or weight-ratio considerations.

items.question: Does GIA give fancy-shaped diamonds an overall cut grade?
items.answer: GIA’s traditional overall cut grade applies to qualifying standard Round Brilliant diamonds. Fancy shapes still receive measurements, polish, symmetry and a girdle description.

items.question: What does Thin to Thick mean?
items.answer: It means the thinnest relevant area is Thin and the thickest is Thick.

items.question: Can I average Thin and Thick as Medium?
items.answer: No. The range describes two extremes and must not be converted into an assumed average verbal category.

items.question: Why does a diamond’s girdle vary?
items.answer: Variation can result from normal scalloping, shape design, facet placement, painting, digging, retained rough, extra facets or other cutting characteristics.

items.question: What is a faceted girdle?
items.answer: It is a girdle divided into a series of small polished surfaces.

items.question: Is a faceted girdle better?
items.answer: Not automatically. It is a finish style and does not guarantee better cut, durability or value.

items.question: What is a polished girdle?
items.answer: It is a smooth polished girdle without separately visible small girdle facets.

items.question: What is a bruted girdle?
items.answer: A bruted girdle has a frosted or granular surface produced during the shaping process.

items.question: Is a bruted girdle bad?
items.answer: No. It can be acceptable and may be historically appropriate for an antique diamond.

items.question: What is a bearded girdle?
items.answer: A bearded girdle contains very small feather-like features extending from the girdle surface into the diamond.

items.question: Does a bearded girdle affect clarity?
items.answer: It can, depending on its extent, depth and visibility.

items.question: What is painting on a diamond girdle?
items.answer: Painting is a cutting technique that alters the relationship between half facets, bezel facets, pavilion mains and girdle thickness.

items.question: What is digging out?
items.answer: Digging out is the opposite facet-angle relationship from painting and creates a different variation between girdle junctions.

items.question: Are painting and digging always defects?
items.answer: No. Minimal examples may have limited significance, while stronger examples can affect appearance and cut grade.

items.question: What is a natural on the girdle?
items.answer: It is a portion of the original rough surface intentionally left on the polished diamond.

items.question: Is a girdle natural the same as damage?
items.answer: No. It is retained rough surface, although its size, depth and location still require assessment.

items.question: What is an indented natural?
items.answer: It is retained rough surface extending below the intended polished outline of the diamond.

items.question: What is a chipped girdle?
items.answer: It is accidental missing material along the diamond’s edge.

items.question: Can a chipped girdle be repaired?
items.answer: Repolishing or recutting may be possible, but it can reduce carat weight and alter proportions. Professional assessment is required.

items.question: Can a diamond chip while being set?
items.answer: Yes. Setting pressure can damage an extremely thin edge, vulnerable corner or area affected by an inclusion.

items.question: Can a diamond girdle be damaged during normal wear?
items.answer: Yes. Severe impact, worn prongs, contact with other diamonds or movement in the setting can damage the girdle.

items.question: What is a girdle inscription?
items.answer: It is microscopic text, numbers or symbols applied to the girdle, often including a grading-report number.

items.question: Does a laser inscription prove authenticity?
items.answer: No. It supports identification but must be checked against the report, measurements and diamond characteristics.

items.question: Can a girdle inscription be removed?
items.answer: It may be removed or reduced if the girdle is repolished.

items.question: Why can’t I see the inscription?
items.answer: It may be hidden by a prong, dirty, extremely small, absent or removed. Proper magnification and lighting are required.

items.question: Does every GIA natural diamond have an inscription?
items.answer: No. Inscription availability depends on the report service and whether the service was requested or included.

items.question: Can girdle thickness identify a natural diamond?
items.answer: No. Natural and laboratory-grown diamonds can have similar girdle thicknesses and finishes.

items.question: Can a laser inscription identify a laboratory-grown diamond?
items.answer: An applicable laboratory inscription may state that a diamond is laboratory-grown, but the complete report and professional identification should still be verified.

items.question: Are GIA and HRD girdle percentages the same?
items.answer: No. Their terminology, measurement structures and grading systems must be interpreted separately.

items.question: Is girdle thickness more important than overall cut?
items.answer: No. It is one part of the diamond’s durability, weight ratio and craftsmanship assessment.

items.question: Should I reject a diamond because its girdle is Very Thin?
items.answer: Not automatically. Determine the location, extent, condition, shape, setting and price before deciding.

items.question: Should I reject a diamond because its girdle is Very Thick?
items.answer: Not automatically. Compare its face-up dimensions, total depth, appearance and price with similar diamonds.
